senses.definition: To move your body to a rhythm, usually in time with music.
examples: They danced until the band packed up.
She learned to dance the tango in Buenos Aires.

senses.definition: A series of movements performed to music, or a social event where people dance.
examples: The final dance of the evening was a waltz.
There is a village dance every Saturday in summer.

note: The pronunciation ˈdɑː.tə is also common in British English.

senses.definition: Facts, measurements, or information, especially when collected for analysis.
examples: The data suggest a slow but steady recovery.
We anonymise all customer data before analysis.
He spent a week cleaning the data before running the model.

senses.definition: To choose something after thinking about the possibilities.
examples: We decided to take the train instead of flying.
She still has not decided which offer to accept.
The committee will decide on Friday.

note: Both ˈaɪ.ðə and ˈiː.ðə are heard in Britain; ˈiː.ðɚ dominates in the United States.

senses.definition: One or the other of two people or things.
examples: You can park on either side of the road.
Either answer would have been acceptable.

senses.definition: Used after a negative statement to mean 'also'.
examples: I did not enjoy the film, and my brother did not either.
She cannot come, and he cannot either.

senses.definition: A serious and determined attempt to do something, especially something difficult.
examples: The expedition was a remarkable endeavour.
Scientific endeavour depends on patient, unglamorous work.

senses.definition: To try hard to do or achieve something.
examples: We endeavour to reply to every message within a day.
She endeavoured to keep her voice steady.

note: A rare case where the American form has an extra /j/ glide that the British form lacks.

senses.definition: A number, especially one that forms part of official statistics.
examples: The latest unemployment figures were published today.
Sales reached six figures for the first time.

senses.definition: The shape of a person's body, or a person seen at a distance.
examples: A tall figure appeared at the end of the corridor.
He is a well-known figure in local politics.

note: British English usually stresses the first syllable; American English the second.

senses.definition: A building where a car is kept, usually next to or part of a house.
examples: The bikes are in the garage behind the house.
We converted the garage into a small office.

senses.definition: A business that repairs or sells cars and often sells fuel.
examples: The garage said the gearbox needs replacing.
Stop at the garage on the corner and fill up.

senses.definition: Real and exactly what it appears to be; not fake.
examples: The certificate turned out to be genuine after all.
These are genuine leather, not a substitute.
She showed genuine concern for the family.
There was genuine surprise on his face.

note: American English typically drops the initial /h/; British English keeps it.

senses.definition: A plant whose leaves or seeds are used to flavour food or as a medicine.
examples: Add a handful of fresh herbs at the end of cooking.
She grows herbs in pots on the windowsill.
Mint is the easiest herb for a beginner to keep alive.

senses.definition: A place where ill or injured people are treated and cared for.
examples: He spent three nights in hospital after the accident.
The new children's hospital opens next spring.
She drove her neighbour to the hospital at two in the morning.

senses.definition: To move or do something more quickly than usual.
examples: If we hurry, we can still catch the last ferry.
Do not hurry the decision; take the week you were given.

senses.definition: The need or wish to do something quickly.
examples: There is no hurry, the deadline is next month.
In her hurry she left the keys in the door.
